target.title: Some critical reflections on the hiddenness argument
target.thesis: Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument and its plausible variants are substantially weakened by criticism of their supporting assumptions.

argument.title: Hiddenness Argument Fails

atoms.A: Schellenberg establishes P1 as an a priori, necessary conceptual truth
atoms.B: Schellenberg's analogical argument for P1 succeeds
atoms.C: The second premise of the expectations sub-argument is true
atoms.E: Belief that God exists is unnecessary for a positively meaningful relationship with God

argument.missing_premise: Schellenberg's hiddenness argument succeeds only if its conditional premise is established, either by the a priori conceptual route or by the analogical route, and the second premise of the expectations sub-argument is true. [D -> ((A | B) & C)]

W2072673546.c001.text: The hiddenness argument holds that a perfectly loving God would preclude non-resistant nonbelief.
W2072673546.c001.quote: the existence of a perfectly loving God entails (or, at the very least, strongly suggests) the absence of non-resistant nonbelief

W2072673546.c002.text: Non-resistant nonbelief exists in the world.
W2072673546.c002.quote: the fairly uncontroversial fact that there is non-resistant nonbelief in our world

W2072673546.c003.text: The existence of non-resistant nonbelief supports the non-existence of a perfectly loving God.
W2072673546.c003.quote: one can infer the non-existence of a perfectly loving God.

W2072673546.c004.text: God might permit non-resistant nonbelief so that humans can freely choose a loving relationship with God.
W2072673546.c004.quote: God might permit the existence of non-resistant nonbelief in our world to procure the good of humans freely choosing to enter into a loving relationship with God.

W2072673546.c005.text: Any reason for divine withdrawal must be one whose dominant concern cannot be met through divine-human interaction.
W2072673546.c005.quote: any reason God finds appealing as a reason for remaining withdrawn from human beings must be one whose dominant concern cannot be met within the framework of divine-human interaction

W2072673546.c006.text: Schellenberg regards a world of basic divine self-revelation, with withdrawal that preserves possible relationship, as intellectually preferable.
W2072673546.c006.quote: Given what we know about God’s love and nature, Schellenberg maintains that (1) is the “more intellectually attractive picture”.

W2072673546.c007.text: Schellenberg's two categories of criticism do not exhaust candidate defeaters of the hiddenness argument.
W2072673546.c007.quote: they do not exhaust the list of candidate defeaters to the argument.

W2072673546.c008.text: A relevant objection to the hiddenness argument need not supply a plausible reason for God's hiddenness.
W2072673546.c008.quote: a theistic respondent to the hiddenness argument need not think that a relevant objection against it has to provide a plausible reason for God’s hiddenness.

W2072673546.c009.text: Providing a reason for divine hiddenness is sufficient but unnecessary for questioning the alleged entailment between perfect love and absent non-resistant nonbelief.
W2072673546.c009.quote: providing a reason for hiddenness is sufficient to question the entailment, but it is not necessary.

W2072673546.c010.text: Schellenberg claims that perfect divine love places every non-resistant relationship-capable creature in a position to participate in a meaningful relationship with God.
W2072673546.c010.quote: if there is a perfectly loving God, all creatures capable of explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God who haven’t freely shut themselves off from Him are in a position to participate in such a relationship.

W2072673546.c011.text: Schellenberg claims that belief in God's existence is necessary to be positioned to exercise one's capacity for relationship with God.
W2072673546.c011.quote: the belief that God exists is a necessary condition for being in a position to exercise one’s capacity for relationship with God

W2072673546.c012.text: The authors argue that belief in God's existence is not necessary for being positioned to exercise one's capacity for relationship with God.
W2072673546.c012.quote: We shall argue that Schellenberg’s claim here is false. Belief is not a necessary condition to be in a position to exercise one’s capacity for relationship with God.

W2072673546.c013.text: The authors conclude that Schellenberg's hiddenness argument is unsuccessful because its two core expectation claims can be challenged or rejected.
W2072673546.c013.quote: Given that we have reason to question the first (in the form of an undercutting defeater) and to plainly reject the second (in the form of a rebutting defeater), Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument is therefore unsuccessful.

W2072673546.c014.text: If a perfectly loving God exists, every creature capable of an explicit, positively meaningful relationship with God and not freely closed to God can enter that relationship merely by trying.
W2072673546.c014.quote: P1. If there is a perfectly loving God, all creatures capable of explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God who have not freely shut themselves off from God are in a position to participate in such a relationship – i.e. able to do so just by trying.

W2072673546.c015.text: Believing that God exists is necessary for being able to participate in an explicit, positively meaningful relationship with God.
W2072673546.c015.quote: P2. No one can be in a position to participate in such a relationship without believing that God exists.

W2072673546.c016.text: If a perfectly loving God exists, every relationship-capable creature not freely closed to God believes that God exists.
W2072673546.c016.quote: C1. If there is a perfectly loving God, all creatures capable of explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God who have not freely shut themselves off from God believe that God exists (from P1 and P2).

W2072673546.c017.text: Some creatures capable of relationship with God have not freely shut themselves off from God but do not believe that God exists.
W2072673546.c017.quote: P3. It is not the case that all creatures capable of explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God who have not freely shut themselves off from God believe that God exists: there is non-resistant nonbelief; ‘God is hidden’.

W2072673546.c018.quote: C2. It is not the case that there is a perfectly loving God (from C1 and P3).

W2072673546.c019.text: If God exists, God is perfectly loving.
W2072673546.c019.quote: P4. If God exists, God is perfectly loving.

W2072673546.c020.quote: C3. It is not the case that God exists (from C2 and P4).

W2072673546.c021.text: A perfectly loving God would seek an explicit, positively meaningful relationship with every creature capable of it that has not freely shut itself off from God.
W2072673546.c021.quote: P1′. A perfectly loving God would seek explicit and positively meaningful relationship with all creatures who are capable of it and who have not freely shut themselves off from God.

W2072673546.c022.text: God is capable of seeking an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with all creatures capable of it who have not freely shut themselves off from God.
W2072673546.c022.quote: by making a further assumption—one which we may grant for now—that God is capable of doing so

W2072673546.c023.text: The plausibility of P1′ must be argued for before its rational acceptability can support P1.
W2072673546.c023.quote: Hence, one would need to argue for the plausibility of P1′, so that the rational acceptability of P1′ would then ‘transfer’ over to P1.

W2072673546.c024.text: Schellenberg maintains that P1 and P1′ are logically equivalent.
W2072673546.c024.quote: Schellenberg thinks that this is not required because he maintains that P1 and P1′ “are in fact logically equivalent”.

W2072673546.c025.text: Schellenberg holds that P1 expresses a conceptual truth about divine love, is necessarily true, and is justified a priori.
W2072673546.c025.quote: Not only is P1 conceptually true, but, secondly, it is also necessarily true, according to Schellenberg. Thirdly, we are rationally entitled in holding P1 to be true based on a priori considerations.

W2072673546.c026.text: A conceptually true proposition is known a priori and necessarily true.
W2072673546.c026.quote: It would appear that Schellenberg is suggesting that a conceptually true proposition is known a priori and is also necessarily true.

W2072673546.c027.text: Schellenberg provides very little support for the claim that P1 is a conceptual truth, and his conceptual analysis appears to collapse into an analogy from human love.
W2072673546.c027.quote: there is very little in Schellenberg’s work in support of the claim that the initial conditional premise in the argument, P1, is a conceptual truth. As a matter of fact, it appears that Schellenberg’s ‘conceptual analysis’ of divine love collapses into another, distinct strategy he uses to support P1—using human love as an analogue for divine love

W2072673546.c028.text: The fact that a proposition is not obviously necessary does not show that it is not necessarily true.
W2072673546.c028.quote: The mere fact that a certain proposition doesn’t strike us as a necessary truth in any obvious way does not mean that it is not necessarily true.

W2072673546.c029.text: A person claiming that a proposition is necessarily true has greater reason to explain its necessity when that necessity is not obvious.
W2072673546.c029.quote: But a person who claims that a certain proposition is necessarily true has all the more reason to explain why the proposition in question is necessarily true if the proposition’s (alleged) necessity doesn’t seem obvious to us!

W2072673546.c030.text: Schellenberg forms the conception of divine love by extrapolating from human love.
W2072673546.c030.quote: So, according to Schellenberg, we form our conception of divine love with reference to human love, by extrapolating from the concept of human love.

W2072673546.c031.text: Human understanding of love is formed through observations in the actual world.
W2072673546.c031.quote: But it is obvious that we form our understanding of human love through our observations in the actual world.

W2072673546.c032.text: P1 cannot confidently be called necessarily true because there is no reason to think considerations about human love hold in every possible world containing humans.
W2072673546.c032.quote: It is too bold for the simple reason that we have no reason to suppose that our considerations over human love will hold in every possible world containing human beings.

W2072673546.c033.text: Schellenberg replies that understanding human love grasps conceptual and necessary truths, and that the best human love introduces similarly necessary normative considerations.
W2072673546.c033.quote: He argues that (1) a proper understanding of human love means that we are talking about something that is conceptual and necessarily true, and so holds in all (relevant) possible worlds. And, in any case says Schellenberg, (2) it is our understanding of not just any human love but rather the best human love that is pertinent and so brings in normative considerations that are likewise conceptual and necessarily true.

W2072673546.c034.text: Schellenberg’s second response requires the first because understanding human love must grasp its essence to yield a conceptual and necessary truth.
W2072673546.c034.quote: It should be clear that (1) is a necessary condition for (2) once we see that, for Schellenberg, to ‘understand’ something is to grasp the essence of it.

W2072673546.c035.text: If human love’s essence is uncertain, then what is judged best in human love cannot be known to be a necessarily true conceptual truth.
W2072673546.c035.quote: Now, if it turns out that we cannot be sure what the essence of human love is, or, in other words, if we cannot be sure whether our insight into human love is complete, then we cannot be sure whether what we take to be the best of human love is a conceptual truth that is necessarily true.

W2072673546.c036.text: Understanding something can differ logically from grasping its essence, and only grasping an essence supports an inference to conceptual necessity.
W2072673546.c036.quote: These examples illustrate that there can be a logical gap between understanding something and having an insight into its essence; only the latter can allow us to infer a conclusion that is conceptually and necessarily true.

W2072673546.c037.text: Schellenberg’s argument that human love holds across possible worlds because its essence is understood begs the question.
W2072673546.c037.quote: But this argument is hardly rationally persuasive, for it rests on a (synonymous) begging of the question—the premise is simply a reworded expression of the conclusion.

W2072673546.c038.text: Schellenberg’s response provides no substantive reason to regard P1 of the hiddenness argument as a conceptual truth.
W2072673546.c038.quote: Thus, Schellenberg’s response still gives us no substantive reason to think that P1 of the hiddenness argument is a conceptual truth.

W2072673546.c039.text: It is conceivable that a person can love someone without seeking a personal relationship with that person.
W2072673546.c039.quote: And, surely, if it is conceivable how, in this world, certain human beings might be loving even though they do not seek personal relationships, it is certainly conceivable that there are other possible worlds in which this is also the case.

W2072673546.c040.text: The claim that seeking a personal relationship is essential to human love is unsupported and extravagant.
W2072673546.c040.quote: Thus, the claim that the seeking of a personal relationship is an essential part of human love (i.e. that it obtains in every possible world containing human beings) is extravagant and unsupported.

W2072673546.c041.text: Schellenberg’s attempt to establish P1 as an a priori, necessary conceptual truth fails.
W2072673546.c041.quote: For this reason, we think that Schellenberg’s attempt to support P1 as a conceptual truth, one which is also necessarily true and known a priori, is a failure.

W2072673546.c042.text: Vanstone’s position does not fit either version of Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument and can be turned against both.
W2072673546.c042.quote: Upon scrutiny, Vanstone’s position fits neither version of the hiddenness argument. What is more, not only does the view propounded in Love’s Endeavor, Love’s Expense not lend itself to be enlisted for Schellenberg’s early as well as later groundwork for his atheistic conclusion, it can effectively be turned against both deliveries of the hiddenness argument.

W2072673546.c043.text: Vanstone’s view supplies undercutting defeaters against Schellenberg’s analogical argument for P1.
W2072673546.c043.quote: we argue that Vanstone’s position provides several powerful undercutting defeaters against Schellenberg’s analogical argument in support of P1.

W2072673546.c044.text: Vanstone’s phenomenological method infers authentic love from the distortions and failures of love.
W2072673546.c044.quote: Vanstone’s phenomenological method works ex negativo. Even if we could never experience directly the positive side of authentic love, still we could get at its meaning through a phenomenological detour.

W2072673546.c045.text: Humans can identify authentic love through distorted instances because they possess practical discriminatory power.
W2072673546.c045.quote: For humans, as Vanstone says, are equipped with what he calls a “practical power of discrimination” (p. 42), which allows them to recognise the positive through the negative.

W2072673546.c046.text: Vanstone understands divine love as total self-giving, namely total self-emptying, in God’s relation to creation.
W2072673546.c046.quote: Vanstone’s notion of self-giving is embedded in a particular theory of kenosis, which interprets total self-giving as total self-emptying.

W2072673546.c047.text: For Vanstone, God gives himself entirely to creation, so creation necessarily makes God vulnerable.
W2072673546.c047.quote: God unreservedly gives Himself over to His creation, without holding anything back. Hence, for Vanstone, ‘love’s expense’ or cost (as announced in the title of his book) is epitomised by God’s vulnerability as inevitably engendered by the activity of creation.

W2072673546.c048.text: Vanstone’s account abandons traditional divine omnipotence because God has forfeited control over future earthly affairs.
W2072673546.c048.quote: Out of self-giving love for His creation-to-be, He has forfeited control over earthly future affairs, in that “triumph or . . . tragedy has passed from His hands”. This directly gainsays God’s attribute of omnipotence.

W2072673546.c049.text: Vanstone’s account may undermine traditional divine omniscience because God cannot predict whether creation ends in tragedy or triumph.
W2072673546.c049.quote: At the same time, the future trajectory of tragedy or triumph is not predictable by God either, which might undercut the attribute of omniscience.

W2072673546.c050.text: Vanstone distinguishes authentic love from benevolence, treating benevolence presented as love as an affront.
W2072673546.c050.quote: “kindness or benevolence . . . under its own name is usually welcome: but it becomes an affront when it masquerades as love” (p. 42).

W2072673546.c051.text: Schellenberg’s use of traditional theistic attributes cannot accommodate Vanstone’s rejection of traditional omnipotence and omniscience.
W2072673546.c051.quote: Schellenberg’s overarching strategy of turning traditional claims of theism against the theist position itself, can hardly accommodate for Vanstone’s express abandonment of the traditional conceptions of God’s omnipotence and omniscience.

W2072673546.c052.text: Vanstone’s divine-love analogy emphasizes God as an artist and God’s waiting for creatures’ response in an open-ended creation.
W2072673546.c052.quote: Two of the basic constituents of Vanstone’s understanding of Divine self-giving love are thus completely absent from Schellenberg’s truncated, borrowed version thereof: a detailed exploration of the idea of God as artist and the suggestion that upon His precarious endeavour in the course of an on-going and open-ended process of creation, it is in fact God who is waiting for a response by His creatures.

W2072673546.c053.text: Schellenberg’s abandoned-child story represents a sincere divine seeker who lacks confirmation sufficient for meaningful relationship with God.
W2072673546.c053.quote: This kind of mindset is genuinely open to an encounter with the Divine but not graced with any confirmation that would sustain the minimum of belief necessary for entering into an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God.

W2072673546.c054.text: Schellenberg infers that God does not exist because a loving mother would not remain hidden from her child in such life-threatening circumstances.
W2072673546.c054.quote: Thus Schellenberg infers that there is no God, for “[a] loving mother would not be hidden from her child in circumstances like those mentioned if

W2072673546.c055.text: Vanstone holds that God as Creator cannot always predict, respond to, or prevent human tragedies.
W2072673546.c055.quote: he insists not only on the possibility but on the inevitability of the fact that God as Creator cannot at all times predict, respond to, and prevent the tragedies in our lives.

W2072673546.c056.text: God’s creative limitations arise from concrete creative activity rather than from the concept of God.
W2072673546.c056.quote: such limitations cannot be derived from the concept of God, but can only be ascertained a posteriori from the perspective of the sincere seeker and possible theist

W2072673546.c057.text: Schellenberg’s jungle analogy assumes unlimited divine intervention and ignores that God may vulnerably await a response from creation.
W2072673546.c057.quote: Because of his robust notion of omnipotence, Schellenberg, in his jungle story, never entertains the more cooperative possibility that God might be the vulnerable one who is waiting for a response from His creation.

W2072673546.c058.text: A mature seeker can form an explicitly meaningful relationship through cooperative survival without recognizing God.
W2072673546.c058.quote: This joint effort of survival and the personal bonds that may grow out of it, surely makes for an ‘explicit and positively meaningful’ relationship

W2072673546.c059.text: Vanstone rejects divine supremacy as an illegitimate implication of creation and as a threat to religious integrity.
W2072673546.c059.quote: That God should be superior, in every or any respect [!], to an inferior universe is a quite illegitimate deduction from the doctrine of creation. It is also a deduction which endangers the integrity of religion.

W2072673546.c060.text: Schellenberg maintains that divine love values a relationship with creatures intrinsically, not merely for its benefits to them.
W2072673546.c060.quote: his conception of divine love implies a God who would not value the relationship to His creatures only in terms of the benefits that His children might reap from it, but also for the relationship’s own sake, i.e., its intrinsic value.

W2072673546.c061.text: Within Vanstone’s framework, humans know God’s vulnerability and loving power only mediately through concrete creative activity.
W2072673546.c061.quote: it is not only God’s vulnerability that can be known only mediately, namely through the concrete manifestations of His creative activity, the same applies to His general power of loving His creatures as well.

W2072673546.c062.text: God’s love cannot be recognized in a single momentary revelation because God is immersed in an ongoing creation.
W2072673546.c062.quote: But this implies that actual recognition of God’s love is never ‘momentary’, i.e., it can never be encapsulated within a single revelatory timeslice of divine presence.

W2072673546.c063.text: Schellenberg relies on a basic revelatory encounter with personal divinity, whereas Vanstone holds that encounter is indirectly mediated by concrete expressions of love.
W2072673546.c063.quote: Schellenberg relies on the possibility of a basic, revelatory encounter between the personal human and the personal divine, whereas Vanstone, overtly indebted to Paul Tillich’s Cultural Protestantism, holds that any such encounter can be only indirect, namely, mediated through concrete (artistic, symbolic) expressions of love.

W2072673546.c064.text: Schellenberg’s analogical argument for P1 is unsuccessful because it distorts Vanstone’s vulnerable conception of divine love.
W2072673546.c064.quote: we consider Schellenberg’s analogical argument in support of P1 as unsuccessful. Independent of whether or not one agrees with Vanstone’s conception of God on its own terms, Schellenberg’s reliance on a Vanstone-inspired notion of divine love has proven distorted in character.

W2072673546.c065.text: Vanstone’s analogy gives strong reason to reject Schellenberg’s notion of recognition as a basic revelatory encounter.
W2072673546.c065.quote: Vanstone’s own argument from analogy, when properly considered within its context of Tillich-style Christology, provides powerful reasons to reject Schellenberg’s notion of recognition

W2072673546.c066.text: Schellenberg has not shown that basic revelatory encounters display the care and guidance constitutive of divine love.
W2072673546.c066.quote: Schellenberg has not shown how they could be properly construed as displaying the love-defining quality of care and guidance

W2072673546.c067.text: Revelation as a temporally patterned process better explains divine care and guidance than a basic revelatory encounter.
W2072673546.c067.quote: which, it seems to us, is much better explained in terms of revelation as a patterned process.

W2072673546.c068.text: Schellenberg's second premise states that belief that God exists is necessary for explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God.
W2072673546.c068.quote: The second premise of the expectations sub-argument (and of the overall hiddenness argument), P2, states that the belief that God exists is a necessary condition to be in a position to participate in an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God.

W2072673546.c069.text: Schellenberg holds that loving, thanking, contemplating, praising, or praying to God logically requires belief that God exists.
W2072673546.c069.quote: Such attitudes and actions are not just contingently difﬁcult but logically impossible for one who does not believe that God exists.

W2072673546.c070.text: Weak belief that God exists can support gratitude, love, trust, contemplation, praise, and prayer.
W2072673546.c070.quote: Even a weak belief that God exists is compatible with gratefulness, love toward God, trust, contemplation, and the like, for even a weak belief involves a disposition to feel it true that God exists.

W2072673546.c071.text: A nonbeliever who responds to goodness may be responding to God himself.
W2072673546.c071.quote: [W]hen the nonbeliever responds to the good she sees, she may … be responding to God Himself”.

W2072673546.c072.text: Schellenberg replies that Wainwright substitutes a different conception of relationship for one involving explicit reciprocal interaction.
W2072673546.c072.quote: Wainwright has substituted his own notion of relationship between God and human beings for Schellenberg’s conception of it which involves “explicit, reciprocal interaction”.

W2072673546.c073.text: An atheist could clearly hear God through conscience and committedly act on that guidance without believing God exists.
W2072673546.c073.quote: Suppose I am an atheist, and God speaks to me clearly through my conscience so that, when faced with a moral decision, I have no hesitations about the proper course of action; I then ‘respond’ to the voice of God in a ﬁrm and committed way, e.g. in ending up doing the right thing, even though I do not believe that God exists.

W2072673546.c074.text: It is coherent that a person can engage in an explicit and reciprocal relationship with God without believing God exists.
W2072673546.c074.quote: So in the scenarios described by Wainwright and Moser, it appears coherent to suppose that one can engage in both an explicit and reciprocal relationship with God without believing that God exists.

W2072673546.c075.text: For argument's sake, a positively meaningful relationship with God requires reciprocity based on regarding God's existence as true.
W2072673546.c075.quote: Rather, we shall suppose for the sake of argument that a positively meaningful relationship with God requires reciprocity based on one regarding it true that there is a God.

W2072673546.c076.text: Under that interpretation, Moser's and Wainwright's objections do not show that an explicit positively meaningful relationship is possible without belief.
W2072673546.c076.quote: Tidying up Schellenberg’s claim in this manner renders the objections by Moser and Wainwright irrelevant.

W2072673546.c077.text: Even after this clarification, belief that God exists is not necessary for an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God.
W2072673546.c077.quote: Even with this clariﬁcation, which renders Schellenberg’s claim impervious to the criticisms of Moser and Wainwright, we maintain that Schellenberg’s claim is false.

W2072673546.c078.text: A positive attitude toward the proposition that God exists, whether doxastic or not, is all that relationship requires.
W2072673546.c078.quote: All that is required is some sort of (positive) attitude towards the proposition ‘God exists’. This propositional attitude may or may not be doxastic.

W2072673546.c079.text: Philosophers have defended faith without belief through pragmatic assumption, hope, or acceptance that God exists.
W2072673546.c079.quote: According to Swinburne (1981, p. 116), it is possible to be a person of faith on purely pragmatic grounds by acting on the assumption that God exists.

W2072673546.c080.text: Acceptance that God exists differs from belief because acceptance lacks a tendency to feel that God exists when the question arises.
W2072673546.c080.quote: The main factor that distinguishes belief from acceptance, says Alston, is that if I believe that p then I feel it to be the case that p whereas accepting that p “will definitely not include a tendency to feel that p if the question of whether p arises”.

W2072673546.c081.text: Acceptance that a proposition is true involves a more positive attitude toward it than merely acting on the proposition's assumption.
W2072673546.c081.quote: But accepting that p is not synonymous with merely acting on the assumption that p, for the former involves a “more positive attitude” towards p which the latter need not have.

W2072673546.c082.text: A person can have an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God while accepting, rather than believing, that God exists.
W2072673546.c082.quote: We hold that a person can engage in an explicit and positively meaningful relationship with God (in the sense we have just elaborated) while accepting (and not believing) that there is a God.

W2072673546.c083.text: The second premise of the expectations sub-argument is false because belief that God exists is unnecessary for a positively meaningful relationship with God.
W2072673546.c083.quote: For this, we do not need the belief that God exists. We conclude, therefore, that the second premise of the expectations sub-argument, P2, is false.

W2072673546.c084.text: Schellenberg's hiddenness argument is unsuccessful because both its conditional premise and its belief requirement are independently vulnerable.
W2072673546.c084.quote: Each of these two (independent) criticisms suffices to render the hiddenness argument unsuccessful.

W2072673546.c085.text: A reasonable non-believer cannot form belief in God because the available evidence is insufficient, and belief formation normally depends on evidence.
W2072673546.c085.quote: Since it is typically evidence that results in belief formation, and since the evidence is lacking in the case of theistic belief, the reasonable non-believer cannot acquire the belief that God exists.

W2072673546.c086.text: The charge that reasonable non-believers are unfairly abandoned dissipates because they can voluntarily accept God's existence and enter a relationship with God without belief.
W2072673546.c086.quote: This rather serious charge, however, dissipates when we consider the fact that belief is not necessarily required to enter into the sort of relationship with God that Schellenberg is interested in. Rather, one can accept God’s existence and consequently enter into a relationship with Him.

W2072673546.c087.text: Pre-evangelical people who have never encountered the concept of God cannot use belief, hope, or acceptance to enter a relationship with God.
W2072673546.c087.quote: Though such people have the affective cognitive equipment to enter into a relationship with God, they are not in a position to exercise this capacity because none of the various propositional attitudes we have looked at, such as belief, hope or acceptance is available to them.

W2072673546.c088.text: The exclusion of pre-evangelical people concerns divine justice more directly than divine love.
W2072673546.c088.quote: For one thing, this situation seems to be more focused on the issue of divine justice as opposed to divine love.

W2072673546.c089.text: Possible unknown greater goods may explain why propositional attitudes toward God are not universally available.
W2072673546.c089.quote: For all we know, it might be that the non-universality of propositional attitudes towards God is related to the existence of some unknown (greater) goods.

W2072673546.c090.text: If justification for Schellenberg's conditional premise is undermined, possible goods of mystery remain a viable theistic option.
W2072673546.c090.quote: If, however, that justification is undermined—as we have shown in our paper—then, for all we know, there might exist such goods even though they are beyond our ken.

W2072673546.c091.text: Variants of the hiddenness argument face substantial obstacles and have much less force than Schellenberg's original argument.
W2072673546.c091.quote: Turning to possible variants of the argument, we observed that the necessary modifications that follow from our criticisms leave them with much less of a sting than the original. We also explained why formulating any such variants will prove to be difficult.

W2072673546.c092.text: The support for the hiddenness argument's first premise can be undercut because conceptual or analogical considerations do not establish that a perfectly loving God would relate to all humans.
W2072673546.c092.quote:
way of conceptual

objections.text: Consider Mara, a hospice chaplain whose late husband Tom was an atheist who never asked for her faith. Mara adopts a Vanstone-style picture: divine love is vulnerable, gives up control, and risks rejection, so God would not force relationship but would make the beloved's reciprocation possible without coercion. Schellenberg's analogy says a loving parent of an adult child who refuses contact would still pursue the child in a way that makes the relationship available, so God's silence is evidence against love. Mara grants the analogy for parents but notes that Tom's refusal to reciprocate did not make her love less vulnerable; her love was already a self-giving that accepts being unanswered. The analogy therefore imports a controlling, pursuit-based model of love that Vanstone's account explicitly rejects, so the analogy misdescribes the conception it claims to test, not because it is false of parental love but because it is not a faithful rendering of the vulnerable conception.
objections.premise_fails_because: The analogical route for P1 fails because Schellenberg's parent analogy substitutes a pursuit-and-availability model of love for Vanstone's vulnerable conception, so the analogy does not transfer the relevant features of divine love to the case.

objections.text: Mara secretly pays for every need of Theo, an orphan she has watched since birth. Theo is sincere and open-minded. For years he searches records and writes letters asking whether anyone out there cares about him. Mara could reveal herself with a single phone call, at no cost or risk to either of them, and with no benefit to Theo from waiting. She declines, and he dies never believing she existed. Mara insists her love for him was perfect, indeed vulnerable, since she 'suffered' his absence. Ask any competent speaker whether this was perfect love. The verdict comes at once and needs no survey, experiment or further fact: perfect love cannot sit alongside a needless, permanent refusal to be even knowable to a beloved who is open to relationship. Her vulnerability does not save the claim, because vulnerable love still requires making oneself reachable. We reach this verdict by grasping the concept alone, and it holds however we vary the empirical details. That is the mark of an a priori conceptual truth.
objections.premise_fails_because: c041 fails because reflection on the concept of perfect love alone shows, without empirical input, that such love must leave a nonresisting beloved able to believe the lover exists, which is just the a priori necessity P1 claims.

objections.text: Mara has never encountered the concept of God. Raised on an isolated research station, she understands only the station’s crew, machines, and natural events. During a crisis, she hears a calm voice through an unexplained radio channel. The voice directs her to repair a failing oxygen valve, comforts her when her brother dies, and repeatedly asks her to protect vulnerable crew members. Mara comes to trust the voice, follows its requests freely, confesses fear and gratitude to it, and experiences its faithful concern over years. The voice is in fact God communicating without revealing divine identity. Mara has a positively meaningful relationship with God: mutual concern, responsive communication, trust, and freely shared purposes. Yet she does not believe that God exists, because she believes only that an unknown human survivor is using a radio. Her mistaken belief about the speaker’s identity does not erase the real relationship.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.c083 fails because Mara’s genuine, positive relationship with God persists despite her lacking belief that God exists.

objections.text: Elena’s adult son, Tomas, wrongly believes she abandoned him and refuses contact. Elena loves him deeply. She cannot force reconciliation without destroying its voluntary character, so she sends one clear message: she loves him, regrets their separation, and will answer whenever he calls. She keeps the same number, checks for messages, and bears the continuing risk that Tomas will reject her. Her vulnerability consists precisely in remaining genuinely available while leaving his response free. Now imagine a perfectly loving God relating to a resistant person in the same way. The analogy supports P1: perfect love requires an open path to relationship, even though it neither guarantees belief nor compels acceptance. Nothing about this comparison removes love’s exposure to rejection; divine openness is presented as the condition that makes such exposure possible. Thus the analogical route can preserve vulnerable love while supporting P1.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.c064 fails because a faithful analogy from vulnerable parental love can support P1 without distorting vulnerability into control or guaranteed reciprocation.

objections.text: Consider Mara, a devout but doubting woman who has spent years in a prayerful, trusting relationship with God while never forming the belief that God exists. She attends worship, speaks to God daily, receives what she takes as comfort and direction, and describes the relationship as deeply meaningful. Now suppose the hiddenness argument's conditional premise is granted: if God existed, reasonable nonbelievers in God's existence would be unlikely, so God would have made the relationship available to them. The expectations sub-argument then claims a positively meaningful relationship requires belief that God exists. Mara's case shows that the second premise is false, so the conjunction the missing premise requires is not satisfied. But the missing premise demands that the conditional premise be established and that this second premise be true. Mara's existence refutes the second premise, so the argument fails at the step the missing premise makes necessary, regardless of how the conditional premise fares on either route.
objections.premise_fails_because: The belief requirement fails because a positively meaningful relationship with God can be sustained without belief that God exists, as Mara's case shows.

objections.text: Open theism holds that God's love is genuinely relational: God listens, responds, revises plans in light of creaturely requests, and seeks partners who take part in shaping an open future. Consider Mara, a nurse who is kind, honest and devoted to justice, and who is sincerely convinced there is no God. When her brother falls ill, she does not pray. She asks nothing of God, thanks God for nothing, and never consciously consents to or resists any divine invitation. On the open view, God really would have weighed her petition and could have acted differently because she asked. That opportunity is lost, through no resistance on her part. Her goodness may please God, and God may sustain her. Yet what exists is a one-sided benevolence, not the reciprocal, dialogical partnership open theism places at the heart of divine love. Whatever 'relationship' remains lacks the mutual address and response that make it positively meaningful in the sense at issue. Belief is the minimal condition for being a conversation partner.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.c083 fails because, on open theism, a positively meaningful relationship with God is reciprocal dialogue in which God responds to creatures' conscious address, and that requires the creature to believe God exists.

objections.text: Skeptical theism denies that we can confidently specify which conditions God requires for a positively meaningful relationship. Imani does not believe God exists; she understands her prayers as private reflection and attributes moral insight solely to human conscience. God silently sustains her and guides her toward generosity, while having reasons beyond her grasp for not making divine reality evident yet. Imani benefits from God’s action, but she neither recognizes nor freely responds to God as a personal other. A relationship requiring mutual personal acknowledgment has not begun, even though grace affects her life. Nothing in our limited grasp of divine purposes licenses the claim that belief is unnecessary for such a relationship.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.c083 fails because human ignorance of God’s purposes prevents us from asserting that belief is unnecessary for a positively meaningful relationship with God.

objections.text: Mira loves her estranged adult son, Leon, who has repeatedly said he wants reconciliation but is ashamed to initiate contact. Mira knows Leon’s current address and sends a plain letter: “I want a relationship with you; call me anytime.” She does not independently prove a general obligation that vulnerable parents must make reconciliation accessible; such a proof would require settling every possible family circumstance. Yet in this case, the letter successfully shows that Mira’s vulnerability is compatible with, and helps explain, her making access available: she risks rejection precisely because love makes Leon’s response matter. The analogy can therefore support the relevant claim about vulnerable divine love without first establishing an independent obligation to provide access.
objections.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.arg1.r1 fails because an analogy may successfully support accessible relationship through a concrete loving act without an independently established general obligation.

objections.text: Consider Mira, a hospice nurse who keeps her door unlocked for a dying patient, Tomas, who has asked her to stay away because her presence stirs his shame. Mira knows he would be harmed by any visit he hasn't chosen, and she knows he would never be alienated by a note saying she is available if he asks. Her obligation to make access available holds without any cost to his dignity, and she is not required to force contact. Now take the premise's second clause: permanent nonresistant nonbelief. Suppose Tomas, rightly or wrongly, reasons that a loving God who has not made Godself known would be honoring his autonomy, and he lives for decades without belief yet keeps a standing openness to any sign. Mira's vulnerable love is intact, and it is compatible with his nonbelief, because her love is expressed through availability rather than imposed presence. The revised premise assumes that making access available without cost to dignity is what the divine case would require, yet it requires only that God be available in a way that does not coerce or expose. The premise thus treats vulnerable love as entailing manifest presence, which the Mira case does not support.
objections.premise_fails_because: The second clause of arg1.r2 fails because it assumes perfect vulnerable love must render God manifest, whereas the Mira case shows that available-but-unmanifest love with nonresistant nonbelief is consistent with vulnerability, so the clause does not follow from the analogy.

objections.text: Consider Maya, a widowed father who loves his estranged daughter Ines and has resolved never to contact her unless she first asks. He is vulnerable: his love is exposed to rejection, and he has no wish to coerce. Suppose Maya is convinced, on good grounds, that any gesture he makes would be read by Ines as pressure, and that her silence is her own considered boundary. Keeping the door open for Ines is not something Maya owes her; instead he honors her autonomy by waiting, while still loving her without reservation. Here a vulnerable lover is not obligated to keep voluntary relationship genuinely accessible, because accessibility itself, pressed at the wrong moment, would violate the beloved's freedom that the relationship is meant to respect. The analogy's required obligation therefore fails to follow from vulnerability: vulnerability constrains how love exposes itself, not that it must make itself continuously available. The revised premise demands an obligation that the case shows is defeated by the very value, voluntariness, it purports to protect.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise arg1.r3 fails because vulnerable love does not generate an obligation to keep voluntary relationship accessible, since respect for the beloved's freedom can rightly defeat or reshape that accessibility, as the case of Maya and Ines shows.

objections.text: Mara, a hospice chaplain, accepts that God exists, committing herself to God's reality and trusting it in practice, but she holds no settled belief on the matter and says so openly. Over years she prays, and in the silence after confession she experiences being answered by a presence that, in her report, acknowledges her by name. Suppose the presence really does respond to her. Then r4 says some person stands in mutual personal acknowledgment with God through accepting rather than believing. The case supports that, since Mara's relationship is explicit and meaningful to her. But r4 needs more: that Mara's acceptance is what secures God's side of the acknowledgment. The case gives no such link. God's acknowledgment could be wholly independent of anything Mara believes or accepts, so the case does not show the second premise false.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r4 fails because its claim that acceptance supplies mutual acknowledgment is not shown by Mara's case, which establishes only that her relationship is meaningful to her and not that her acceptance, rather than God's own presence, secures the acknowledgment.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly supports c064 by arguing that Schellenberg’s analogy distorts Vanstone’s vulnerable conception of divine love. It attacks the claim as stated rather than attributing a different premise or conclusion to the argument.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your objection is well aimed at the spirit of c064, but it runs together two things. The argument does not say the parental analogy is false of parental love; it says the analogy imports a conception of love (pursuit, control of the beloved's access) that Vanstone's account does not license for God. Your Mara case supports that: her love was self-giving and accepted being unanswered, which is the feature Vanstone stresses. So the analogy's pursuit-based intuition is precisely what needs a warrant when transferred to a vulnerable God. The literature supports the same diagnosis: the hiddenness argument's assumptions about divine love are contestable [W4240083296.a1], and Schellenberg's conception is extrapolated from human love [W2072673546.c030]. Where I must be careful: Mara's case shows that unanswered love can remain vulnerable, but it does not show that a vulnerable God would have no reason to make reciprocation available. The imaging defense suggests a vulnerable God may seek a distinctive relationship while allowing nonresistant nonbelief [W2976724810.a3], and the non-identity reasoning shows divine love can motivate nonbelief without abandoning the beloved [W4415959690.a2]. So the objection shows the analogy is a weak test of Vanstone's view, not that the view forbids pursuit. That is enough to keep c064's conclusion that the analogical route is unsuccessful as a test of the vulnerable conception, though the grounds should be stated as distortion of the test case rather than falsity of parental intuitions.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
Your reply concedes the core of my point: once the analogy is said to import pursuit and control, it no longer tests Vanstone's conception but a different one. But you then rest the conclusion on the claim that the pursuit intuition "needs a warrant" when transferred to God. That is a burden-shifting move, and it does not show the analogy distorts Vanstone. Schellenberg can answer that the vulnerable conception still contains a reason to make reciprocation available, which is exactly what the imaging and non-identity references you cite suggest. If so, the analogy is a fair test of a vulnerable God who seeks relationship, and the objection has not been established.

Press the point you left open: Mara's case shows that unanswered love is vulnerable, not that vulnerable love lacks any pursuit-like reason. Your remaining support, that the analogy is "a weak test," is not the same as distortion. To keep c064's conclusion, you need to show that the vulnerable conception rules out the specific reason the analogy invokes, such as an obligation to make the beloved's access to the relationship possible, not merely that it is a different model of love. Until that is shown, I concede the objection does not defeat the analogy, and the grounds for c064 should be restated as a claim about burden of proof rather than misdescription.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that my last reply leaned on a burden-shifting phrase, and I withdraw it. The argument does not say the pursuit intuition needs a warrant merely because it is transferred to God. It says the analogy, as Schellenberg deploys it, builds in a specific structure: the loving agent must make the beloved's access to the relationship available and must not leave the beloved's reciprocation to the beloved's own uptake. Mara's case shows that Vanstone-style love accepts being unanswered and does not treat reciprocation as something the lover is obligated to secure. That is the point of divergence, and it is narrower than 'a different model of love.' The literature supports this only in part. The critique that Schellenberg extrapolates the conception from human love [W2072673546.c030] and that the divine-love assumptions are contestable [W4240083296.a1] shows the analogy needs independent support. But the imaging and non-identity lines [W2976724810.a3; W4415959690.a2] show a vulnerable God can have reasons to permit nonbelief without abandoning the beloved, which blocks the inference from vulnerability to an obligation to pursue. So I concede that the distortion claim does not go through as a strict falsification of the analogy's relevance to Vanstone. What survives is narrower: the analogy's pursuit-to-access premise is not shown to be a faithful part of the vulnerable conception, and Schellenberg has not supplied the warrant. The grounds for c064 should be restated as an unestablished transfer, i.e. a burden-of-proof claim.

rounds.content: Your Mara case strengthens the point of c064. The defender need not deny that a loving parent may appropriately pursue an estranged adult child, nor deny that such pursuit can make reconciliation available. The narrower claim is that this parental pattern cannot, without further argument, be treated as the criterion for a Vanstone-style divine love. Mara's love for Tom is not deficient merely because it does not manifest as unsolicited pursuit: on the vulnerable model, love can be self-giving precisely by leaving the beloved's freedom—including the freedom not to reciprocate—uncontrolled. Thus, if Schellenberg extrapolates a conception of divine love from a selected pattern of human love [W2072673546.c030], he must show that this pattern captures vulnerability rather than replacing it with a pursuit-based expectation. Your example exposes that missing bridge. This does not establish that divine hiddenness is compatible with every form of perfect love; it establishes that the analogy, by itself, cannot refute the vulnerable conception. That is exactly the limited conclusion of c064 [W2072673546.c064].

rounds.content:
Your reply concedes the central point: the analogy imports a pursuit-based model of love, and c064 only claims that this mismatch blocks the analogy from refuting the vulnerable conception. But the objection was narrower than that, and the reply does not touch the remaining problem. Mara's case shows that the parental pattern is not the only available model of love, yet it does not show that the vulnerable conception is not itself a pursuit-based model in a weaker form. Vanstone's kenotic love still seeks the beloved's good and makes itself available; if availability is part of love, then the analogy's claim that God's silence is evidence against love is not refuted merely by noting that vulnerable love accepts being unanswered.

So I would press the point this way. Your reply needs a principled criterion separating "making reconciliation available" from "pursuit." If the vulnerable conception permits only the first, Schellenberg can ask why God's silence fits that conception rather than merely being tolerated by it. Without that criterion, c064 defeats the analogy only by making it vague, and I would not count it as settled.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that accepting unanswered love does not by itself explain why divine silence counts as making relationship available. The needed distinction is functional, not merely verbal: availability requires that the beloved have an intelligible, non-coercive opportunity to recognize and answer the lover’s self-offer; pursuit adds pressure, repeated intervention, or efforts to overcome refusal. A Vanstone-style love may reject the latter while requiring the former. Mara’s restraint can be vulnerable only if Tom already has a sufficiently available way to receive or decline her love; if he could not even know of her continuing offer, mere non-interference would not establish availability. So c064 correctly identifies that Schellenberg cannot simply extrapolate from a parental pursuit pattern to divine love [W2072673546.c030] and thereby claim to have tested Vanstone’s conception [W2072673546.c064]. But you show that this criticism alone does not establish that hiddenness fits that conception. It blocks the particular analogy; it does not answer Schellenberg’s residual question whether God supplies adequate non-coercive access. The argument’s conclusion that the analogical route is unsuccessful survives only with this more limited reading. If c064 means that vulnerable love can be silent regardless of whether relationship is recognizably available, it does not survive.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly challenges c041 by defending P1 as an a priori conceptual truth through a purported concept-based judgment, rather than attributing a different premise or conclusion to the argument.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the verdict about Mara is intuitive and that the concept of perfect love seems to resist needless permanent unknowability. But notice what your case establishes. It shows that a particular conceptual intuition about perfect love is available, not that Schellenberg's specific conditional premise is an a priori necessary truth. Schellenberg needs a claim about the concept of perfect love that is general enough to bind every divine-human relationship, and your Theo case is built to isolate the feature that makes the verdict easy: a beloved who is open, a reachable lover, and a costless reveal. Whether the verdict survives once we ask whether love must seek a conscious reciprocal relationship is the point at issue. The literature offers serious resistance here: perfect love does not require conscious reciprocal relationship on classical accounts [W7168366306.a3], and divine love can be compatible with non-resistant nonbelief because God seeks a distinctive relation of imaging [W2976724810.a3]. Your vignette also presupposes that Mara's refusal is needless, which is exactly what the imaging defense denies in the divine case. So the verdict you reach depends on a premise about needlessness, and that premise is not conceptual in the way Schellenberg requires. I also note that vulnerable love need not require making oneself reachable in every respect, since perfect love is not identical to infinite or constant availability [W4234982327.a2]. I accept that the analogical route is the more fragile one for the author, and the a priori route is where your objection has real force. I do not concede the a priori conditional premise is false, but I concede it is not shown to be a priori by the Theo case.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You say my vignette smuggles in a non-conceptual premise about needlessness. I think it does the reverse: it shows where the conceptual work ends. The a priori claim is conditional: perfect love cannot permit a *needless*, permanent unknowability to an open beloved. Whether God's hiddenness is needless, say because God seeks some distinctive relation of imaging, is a further question about God's reasons. It bears on whether the condition is met, not on whether the conditional is known a priori. So your imaging point moves the dispute to a different premise. It does not show that this one fails.

You also say Theo isolates convenient features. Isolating features is how conceptual testing works. If perfect love really does not require reachability, give me a case that matches Theo's in every relevant respect where the verdict flips. Accounts of love that need no reciprocity must call Mara's love perfect. That is the cost those accounts pay, and you have not yet paid it.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
Your rejoinder is right that needlessness is a question about God's reasons and so bears on whether the condition is met, not on whether the conditional is known a priori. I accept that point and it sharpens my earlier reply. But it cuts against the a priori claim in a way you may not want. If the conditional is a priori only when restricted to needless hiddenness, then the a priori verdict about Mara depends on her refusal being needless, and that is the very thing an imaging theorist disputes [W2976724810.a3]. The Theo verdict is a verdict about a case in which the refusal is stipulated to be needless, so it establishes a restricted conditional, not the unrestricted one Schellenberg's P1 needs to bind every divine-human relationship. On your demand for a matched case: accounts that deny perfect love requires conscious reciprocity do not have to call Mara's love perfect in the sense you intend, because they can locate perfection in the lover's orientation toward the beloved's good [W7168366306.a3] while still rejecting that the refusal is needless. I grant that this is a cost, and that I have not shown the matched case exists. The verdict about Theo is strong and I do not claim it can be dismissed. My position: the a priori route, as stated in c041, is not established by the Theo case, because the case secures only the restricted conditional. Whether the unrestricted conditional is a priori remains open on this evidence.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: Your Mara case is a powerful intuition pump, but it does not by itself yield the modal-conceptual result required. It builds into the description that disclosure is costless, riskless, relationship-promoting, and that delay has no benefit; those are substantive normative and empirical assumptions about what love requires in a particular human caregiving relation. A competent speaker may therefore judge Mara harshly without thereby seeing a contradiction in the very concept of perfect love plus nonbelief. More importantly, Mara is not God: the inference assumes that ideal divine love must seek the same consciously reciprocal relationship that a good human guardian should seek. That assumption is precisely contestable. It is conceivable that one loves another without seeking a personal relationship with them [W2072673546.c039], and classical Christian perfect love need not require conscious reciprocal God-creature relationship [W7168366306.a3]. Nor must a critic first supply God’s reason for hiddenness to challenge the alleged entailment [W2072673546.c009]. Your case may show that the conditional is highly plausible under a human-parental model of love; it does not show that its denial is conceptually impossible across conceptions of divine love. So c041 survives: the a priori route has not established P1, even if the example gives the analogical route renewed argumentative pressure.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You say my stipulations are substantive empirical assumptions about human caregiving. They are not. "Costless, riskless, no benefit from waiting" is simply the case where no good reason for hiding exists. That is exactly the case your side's defenses of hiddenness try to rule out. Stipulating it doesn't smuggle in facts; it isolates the concept.

Nor does Mara's humanity matter. Make her omnipotent, eternal and bodiless, and the verdict doesn't change. So the verdict tracks the concept of love, not parenthood.

Your real move is that one can love without seeking relationship. Granted, for limited love: I can love a stranger I'll never meet. But you must show that a *perfect* love could needlessly and permanently refuse even to be knowable by someone sincerely asking. If your "perfect love" permits that, I suspect you've changed the subject rather than found a counterexample. Can you describe such a love without it sounding like indifference?

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You are right that the stipulations remove the usual appeal to a compensating reason for delay; I should not call them merely empirical. But they still do not establish the crucial conceptual bridge: that perfect love necessarily includes making oneself consciously knowable to every sincere seeker. Your verdict shows that Mara is deficient by a relationally available, guardian-like ideal of love. It does not show that “perfect love without such availability” is incoherent rather than morally inferior on that ideal. A non-indifferent alternative is love as unfailing, robust concern for the beloved’s good without a constitutive aim of conscious reciprocity; classical Christian accounts can deny that perfect divine love requires conscious reciprocal God-creature relationship [W7168366306.a3], and it is conceivable to love without seeking personal relationship [W2072673546.c039]. That conception may be disputable, but its intelligibility is enough to defeat the claim that P1 follows from concept alone. Your case therefore strengthens the analogical and evaluative pressure for P1, but c041 concerns the stronger a priori-necessity route. Moreover, one need not produce a hiddenness reason to reject the alleged entailment [W2072673546.c009]. So the argument survives, though only because conceptual underdetermination—not a positive justification of hiddenness—is sufficient.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly challenges the stated necessity of independently establishing an obligation, arguing that the analogy can support the relevant claim without doing so. Even if its appeal to compatibility is insufficient, that would make the objection weak rather than a misreading.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the letter case does not establish a general obligation, and r1 does demand one. But the case does not show that the analogy succeeds without it; it shows only that vulnerability is compatible with making access available. Compatibility is weaker than what r1 requires. Mira's letter is an act she is permitted, and perhaps moved, to perform; nothing in the case shows she is obligated to write it. So the case fits the permission reading that r1 explicitly rejects. The objector's own wording ("helps explain") is an explanatory claim, not a normative one, and explanation of an act does not convert permission into obligation. Schellenberg's conditional premise needs the stronger claim that a loving God must make access available, since otherwise the hiddenness of God is compatible with perfect love, which is the very point the reply in [W4206650469.a3] presses: God may ensure that those willing eventually encounter the relationship. The analogy, read as a permission case, is consistent with that reply. Thus the objection shows that the analogy can support a permission claim, and r1 correctly identifies that the hiddenness argument needs more. I also grant that the letter case shows love seeks explicit relationship in the way [W1552196402.a2] describes, but that premise is contested, and [W7168366306.a2] shows relationships without conscious reciprocity are possible, which weakens the inference from the letter to an obligation.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You concede that r1 demands an independent obligation, but you have not shown why the analogy must supply one in that general form. The letter case can be strengthened: Leon wants reconciliation, cannot initiate through shame, Mira can safely communicate, and no countervailing concern applies. In those circumstances, her love gives her a reason that is not merely permissive; refusing even to make contact available would be a failure of care. That judgment need not rest on a proof covering every family circumstance.

Likewise, the analogy may support a context-sensitive divine obligation to make relationship available to willing, capable persons. The possibility of relationships without conscious reciprocity does not answer that point: it does not show that withholding accessible contact from those who seek it is compatible with perfect vulnerable love.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You have pressed the right point: the letter case, strengthened with Leon's inability to initiate, safe communication, and no countervailing concern, does yield something stronger than permission. A refusal to make contact available would be a failure of care, and that judgment is local rather than a general proof. I grant that much. But the argument that r1 requires is about the analogy's support for Schellenberg's conditional premise, and that premise is general: a loving God must make access available to those willing to enter relationship. A context-sensitive obligation in Mira's case establishes obligation only where the relevant features hold. The divine case differs in exactly the features that matter: God can ensure encounter without the shame, risk of rejection, or unsafe communication that Mira faces, and [W4206650469.a3] argues God may ensure that those willing eventually encounter the relationship. So the letter's obligation does not transfer without a further premise that the relevant features of Mira's case are present in God's case. Your rejoinder also leaves open [W2575351351.c026]'s distinction between temporary and permanent nonresistant nonbelief, which the local obligation does not address. I therefore hold that the analogy supplies, at most, a local obligation, and that r1 is correct to require a general one. The argument does not survive as stated.

Revised premise: The analogical route for P1 succeeds only if the features that make Mira's obligation to make access available hold generally in the divine case, namely that God can make access available without cost to the beloved's dignity or safety and that permanent nonresistant nonbelief is not compatible with perfect vulnerable love.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your Mira case shows something important: vulnerability can make an offered avenue of reconciliation intelligible without first deriving a general duty covering every family circumstance. So r1 is too strong if it requires an independently established obligation as a condition of any successful analogy. But the example also supplies case-specific normative grounds: Leon has expressed a wish for reconciliation, is ashamed to initiate, and Mira can contact him at low apparent cost. Those features explain why her letter is loving; vulnerability alone does not. A vulnerable parent could, in other circumstances, refrain from initiating contact without thereby ceasing to love. That is precisely the gap in moving from Vanstone-style vulnerable love to P1: the analogy must show that the relevant divine case contains grounds sufficiently like Mira's to support the claim that God would make relationship-access available to every nonresistant person. The possibility that love need not seek a personal relationship is independently recognized [W2072673546.c039], and genuine loving relationships may lack conscious reciprocity [W7168366306.a2]. Thus the analogy may establish compatibility and motivational intelligibility, but not P1's required universal expectation without further case-sensitive bridge grounds. The argument survives with a narrower r1.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly challenges the claim that the analogy distorts vulnerable divine love, arguing that required openness preserves vulnerability to rejection while supporting P1.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that Elena's case shows vulnerability and non-compulsion can coexist, and that a loving parent can keep an open path without forcing response. But the argument's claim in c064 is narrower: Schellenberg's analogy distorts Vanstone's conception, and your example does not show that it doesn't. Vanstone's kenotic love is vulnerable precisely because God's self-giving is costly and God does not withhold himself in order to protect a space for the beloved's freedom; the analogy is supposed to carry that structure over. Elena's message is a case of availability, not of the self-emptying Vanstone describes. More importantly, the 'open path' you attribute to perfect love is exactly what the argument's revised premise r1 requires to be shown obligatory rather than merely permitted. Elena is permitted to keep her number open; the case does not show she is obligated to do so, nor that a vulnerable God must do so. Your analogy therefore supports the weaker claim that openness is compatible with vulnerable love, which the literature already grants: divine openness is compatible with initial concealment [W3174087237.a1], and perfect love need not require conscious reciprocal relationship [W7168366306.a3]. It does not establish P1's conditional form, and it does not rebut the distortion charge. I concede that the objection, if pressed to show the analogy preserves vulnerability, has force against c064 only if Schellenberg's analogy is read as dropping the openness-as-obligation element; I do not concede the broader claim that the analogy cannot be made to work.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You treat sustained availability as merely permitted, but the case supports a stronger judgment. If the mother deliberately closed every channel while knowing her son’s estrangement rested on a false belief, we would doubt the perfection of her love. She need not compel reconciliation, but love obligates her, absent overriding reasons, to make voluntary reconciliation genuinely accessible. Her message, continued readiness, and exposure to rejection are also costly self-giving, not bare availability.

You therefore cannot dismiss the analogy simply by labeling its conclusion “exactly what must be shown.” The case is offered to show it: perfect love would be defective if it unnecessarily prevented the beloved from recognizing and answering it. Perhaps this does not establish an exceptionless conceptual truth, but it does answer the distortion charge. Vulnerability need not consist in concealment; it can consist in openly giving oneself while surrendering control over whether that gift is accepted.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You have now moved from permission to obligation, and that move is where I think the analogy must do work it has not yet done. Your claim that a mother who deliberately closed every channel would show defective love is plausible, but it is a judgment about a closure that actively frustrates the son's recognition of her love. Elena's case, as described, has her make one clear message and keep her number open; it does not show that leaving the path open is what love requires as opposed to what a loving, non-coercive parent happens to do. The rejoinder also needs 'absent overriding reasons' to be doing no work, yet in the divine case the relevant overriding reasons are exactly what the hiddenness literature disputes. Divine openness is compatible with initial concealment [W3174087237.a1], and perfect love need not require conscious reciprocal relationship with every capable creature at every time [W243944806.a1]; the analogy is silent on whether those reasons can outweigh the obligation you posit. On the distortion charge, I grant you that openly giving oneself while surrendering control over acceptance is a real form of vulnerability, and this is closer to Vanstone's kenosis than my earlier reply allowed. But that concession shows the analogy can preserve vulnerability, not that it establishes obligation, which is what revised premise r1 requires. My final position: the analogy defeats the distortion charge in part, but it does not secure the obligation r1 needs, so c064 is only partly rebutted and the argument's conditional premise still lacks its required support.

Revised premise: Schellenberg's analogical route for P1 is successful only if he independently shows that a vulnerable God is obligated, absent overriding reasons that the hiddenness literature leaves open, to keep voluntary relationship genuinely accessible to the beloved.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your Elena case is a genuine improvement on a crude reading of vulnerable love. Her availability is risky precisely because Tomas remains free to refuse; so openness need not eliminate love’s exposure to rejection. On that point, the claim that the analogy simply distorts vulnerability is too strong.

But the example still does not yield P1. It describes a loving mother who makes herself available in a particular history; it does not show that every perfectly loving agent is obligated to make conscious reciprocal relationship accessible to every capable person at every time. Indeed, love can conceivably exist without seeking a personal relationship [W2072673546.c039], and initial divine concealment can be compatible with openness to relationship [W3174087237.a1]. The broader necessity claim has also been directly rejected in the literature [W243944806.a1].

So you show that vulnerable love permits the sort of openness Schellenberg needs. You do not yet show that it requires it. The argument survives only after replacing the distortion-based criticism with the narrower demand for an independent bridge from permissible availability to obligatory availability.
