rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly disputes c083’s stated claim that belief in God is unnecessary for a positively meaningful relationship with God. It argues that without belief or recognition of God as a personal other, the relevant relationship has not begun; this attacks the premise as stated rather than substituting a different claim.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your case turns on the word 'explicit.' The argument's claim, following [W2072673546.c082] and [W2072673546.c077], is that a person can have an explicit and positively meaningful relationship while accepting rather than believing that God exists. Imani, as you describe her, lacks acknowledgment of God as a personal other, so she falls outside the claim's scope; c083 is not refuted by a case in which mutual personal acknowledgment is absent. Your skeptical-theist point does real work, though. Skeptical theism [W2417264168.a2] blocks the inference from our inability to see God's reasons to a confident verdict that belief is unnecessary, and I concede that our limited grasp of divine purposes cannot settle which conditions God requires. But the argument does not need that verdict about all persons. It needs only that the conditions for explicit relationship can be met by some believer-free person, which the cited acceptance case supports. The objection's strongest move is the claim that 'nothing in our limited grasp licenses' the unnecessity claim. Here I think the argument must narrow: it does not claim we know belief is unnecessary in every possible case, only that it is unnecessary for the explicit relationship the expectations sub-argument concerns. Against Stump's observation that God can have a personal relationship with non-believers [W4221131558.a1], the hiddenness literature treats this as contested rather than settled, so the argument's c083 is defensible but depends on the acceptance case, not on any general account of divine requirements.
rounds.revised_premise: Belief that God exists is unnecessary for an explicit, positively meaningful relationship with God, where that claim is established by the acceptance case rather than by any general account of which conditions God requires.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: Your narrowed claim still needs support. A person who merely accepts God’s existence for practical purposes, while withholding belief, may not genuinely recognize God as a personal other or be able to offer the trust and reciprocal response a relationship requires. Calling that relation “explicit” does not establish that it has the relevant interpersonal character. More importantly, skeptical theism blocks not only a universal verdict about divine requirements, but also your existential assertion that God could relate positively to some nonbeliever without belief. For all we know, God may have reasons to require belief even where acceptance permits religious practice. The acceptance case therefore describes a possibility only by assuming the disputed point: that belief is dispensable for mutual personal relationship.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that Imani, as described, is not a case of explicit relationship: she neither recognizes God as a personal other nor responds to him as one. That falls outside c083's scope, which concerns the explicit relationship defined in [W2072673546.c082] and [W2072673546.c077], not the grace she receives. Your rejoinder presses harder: acceptance may not supply the interpersonal character a relationship needs, and skeptical theism [W2417264168.a2] blocks any existential claim that God does relate to some believer-free person. I concede the second point in part. Our inability to see God's reasons does leave open that God requires belief for personal relationship, so I cannot establish the existential claim by appeal to divine purposes. The acceptance case must instead be shown, on its own terms, to contain the mutual acknowledgment that a personal relationship requires. The literature does not yet show that; the contested status Stump's view has [W4221131558.a1] reflects this. So c083 as stated does not survive without that further argument. Against this, the hiddenness literature offers [W2575351351.c002], which denies that belief-free relationship is possible at all, and it is that thesis, not skeptical theism, which the acceptance case must answer.

Revised premise: The second premise of the expectations sub-argument is false because some person can, by accepting rather than believing that God exists, stand in mutual personal acknowledgment with God, so that belief is unnecessary for explicit, positively meaningful relationship with God.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: Your Imani case rightly shows that divine action upon someone who neither recognizes nor responds to God as personal other is not yet the relevant kind of relationship. But that is not the case c083 relies on. The proposed alternative to belief is not private reflection mistakenly labelled prayer; it is acceptance that God exists, which can ground an explicit and positively meaningful relationship even where belief is absent [W2072673546.c082]. Thus the author can grant that Imani, as described, lacks such a relationship without granting that belief is necessary for one. Skeptical theism may counsel caution about God’s reasons for hiddenness, but it does not establish the stronger necessity claim that only belief can support mutual personal acknowledgment. Indeed, the argument expressly distinguishes belief’s necessity for explicit relationship from the possibility of explicit relationship on acceptance [W2072673546.c015] [W2072673546.c077]. So your example leaves the decisive alternative unaddressed.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You shift from belief to “acceptance,” but you do not explain how acceptance can sustain mutual personal acknowledgment while belief is absent. If acceptance involves treating God as real enough to address, trust, and freely respond to as a personal other, it seems to include the practical commitment that God exists which the premise calls belief. If it does not, then it may be merely hopeful participation or acting-as-if, and you have not shown that it constitutes a positively meaningful reciprocal relationship rather than unilateral divine action. My Imani case was meant to expose precisely this gap: divine guidance and human receptivity are insufficient without recognized personal encounter. Skeptical theism reinforces the point: you cannot confidently declare that God may enter such a relationship on acceptance alone, rather than requiring belief or later disclosure.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that merely receiving grace, or acting hopefully as if God exists, would not establish mutual personal acknowledgment; Imani therefore lacks the relationship at issue. The author’s intended claim is stronger: acceptance, rather than belief, can coexist with an explicit and positively meaningful relationship [W2072673546.c082], notwithstanding the claim that belief is necessary for explicit relationship [W2072673546.c015]. But your rejoinder exposes that this assertion needs an account of acceptance. If acceptance includes only practical reliance while withholding belief, the author must show how it supports free address, trust, and response to God as an other. If it instead entails those attitudes because it commits one to God’s existence, the distinction from belief requires defense. Citing the possibility of acceptance cannot by itself settle either issue [W2072673546.c077]. Skeptical theism does not prove belief necessary, but it does reinforce the author’s lack of warrant to announce the contrary necessity-denial on the basis given. So c083 does not presently survive: it has identified a possible alternative attitude, not established that it can constitute the required reciprocal relationship.

The objection reads the missing premise correctly: success requires the expectations sub-argument's second premise to be true. Mara is a serious challenge to that premise, since she has years of conscious, meaningful relationship without believing God exists, which fits the premise that nonresistant nonbelievers can have meaningful relationship with God [W2575351351.c004]. The argument's own conclusion already concedes that the belief requirement is vulnerable, and desire without belief is a live model [W2592574756.a1]. Your case is therefore not a refutation of the argument but a confirmation of its failure at the belief step. I would press one reply on Schellenberg's behalf. The second premise is stated as necessity for an explicit, positively meaningful relationship [W2072673546.c068], and Mara's case turns on whether her relationship is explicit in that sense, which depends on whether she has some implicit belief or only desire. That question is open, but it is a contest over the premise's scope, not a showing that the argument survives. Given that, the expectations route fails if Mara's relationship counts as explicit and meaningful, and the conditional premise must carry the argument alone, which the analogical route has not secured.

Revised premise: The expectations sub-argument's second premise must be restricted to explicit relationship in a sense that excludes nonbelieving relationships like Mara's, and that restriction must be independently defended.

rounds.content: You are right that, if Mara is possible, the expectations sub-argument’s belief requirement fails. But that is not a defect in the missing premise; it is one of the two independent vulnerabilities that premise identifies. The argument says Schellenberg’s hiddenness argument succeeds only if both its conditional premise is established and belief in God’s existence is necessary for a positively meaningful relationship. Mara is offered to show that the latter condition is not met, regardless of whether the conditional premise can be secured. So your case supports, rather than defeats, the inference to the conclusion. The author’s position is explicitly that belief is not logically required for relating to God [W2072673546.c093] and is unnecessary even for an explicit, positively meaningful relationship [W2072673546.c077]. Indeed, the paper’s stated conclusion is that the expectations sub-argument’s second premise is false for this reason [W2072673546.c083]. Mara’s prayer, trust, worship, and experienced comfort are therefore relevant evidence for the argument’s intended point: a person may participate meaningfully without first forming the belief the expectations argument demands. Whether her experiences genuinely involve God is a separate metaphysical question; the objection as framed grants the relationship, and under that stipulation it confirms the argument’s diagnosis.

You are right that the objection does not defeat the missing premise. My objection assumed the premise's "only if" structure was a defect, but a necessary condition for success that is refuted in one conjunct is exactly what the argument needs. The conclusion, that both conjuncts are "independently vulnerable," is weaker than that, but its claim about the conditional premise rests on the analogical and a priori routes, which Mara does not touch. Mara therefore supports "unsuccessful" but not the claim that the conditional premise is vulnerable. That gap is not a defect in arg1.mp, which only says both must hold. It is a point about whether c084's wording is licensed by c083 alone. I concede the objection as stated.

Its first independent basis is the prior critique that Schellenberg’s a priori conceptual route fails [W2072673546.c041] and that his analogical route fails because it mischaracterizes vulnerable divine love [W2072673546.c064]; its second is the denial that belief is necessary for a positively meaningful relationship [W2072673546.c083]. Thus Mara does not do double duty. She supplies support for one vulnerability, while the route-specific criticisms supply support for the other. objection.text: Consider Mara, a hospice chaplain whose late husband Tom was an atheist who never asked for her faith. Mara adopts a Vanstone-style picture: divine love is vulnerable, gives up control, and risks rejection, so God would not force relationship but would make the beloved's reciprocation possible without coercion. Schellenberg's analogy says a loving parent of an adult child who refuses contact would still pursue the child in a way that makes the relationship available, so God's silence is evidence against love. Mara grants the analogy for parents but notes that Tom's refusal to reciprocate did not make her love less vulnerable; her love was already a self-giving that accepts being unanswered. The analogy therefore imports a controlling, pursuit-based model of love that Vanstone's account explicitly rejects, so the analogy misdescribes the conception it claims to test, not because it is false of parental love but because it is not a faithful rendering of the vulnerable conception.
objection.premise_fails_because: The analogical route for P1 fails because Schellenberg's parent analogy substitutes a pursuit-and-availability model of love for Vanstone's vulnerable conception, so the analogy does not transfer the relevant features of divine love to the case.

objection.text: Mara secretly pays for every need of Theo, an orphan she has watched since birth. Theo is sincere and open-minded. For years he searches records and writes letters asking whether anyone out there cares about him. Mara could reveal herself with a single phone call, at no cost or risk to either of them, and with no benefit to Theo from waiting. She declines, and he dies never believing she existed. Mara insists her love for him was perfect, indeed vulnerable, since she 'suffered' his absence. Ask any competent speaker whether this was perfect love. The verdict comes at once and needs no survey, experiment or further fact: perfect love cannot sit alongside a needless, permanent refusal to be even knowable to a beloved who is open to relationship. Her vulnerability does not save the claim, because vulnerable love still requires making oneself reachable. We reach this verdict by grasping the concept alone, and it holds however we vary the empirical details. That is the mark of an a priori conceptual truth.
objection.premise_fails_because: c041 fails because reflection on the concept of perfect love alone shows, without empirical input, that such love must leave a nonresisting beloved able to believe the lover exists, which is just the a priori necessity P1 claims.

objection.text: Mara has never encountered the concept of God. Raised on an isolated research station, she understands only the station’s crew, machines, and natural events. During a crisis, she hears a calm voice through an unexplained radio channel. The voice directs her to repair a failing oxygen valve, comforts her when her brother dies, and repeatedly asks her to protect vulnerable crew members. Mara comes to trust the voice, follows its requests freely, confesses fear and gratitude to it, and experiences its faithful concern over years. The voice is in fact God communicating without revealing divine identity. Mara has a positively meaningful relationship with God: mutual concern, responsive communication, trust, and freely shared purposes. Yet she does not believe that God exists, because she believes only that an unknown human survivor is using a radio. Her mistaken belief about the speaker’s identity does not erase the real relationship.
objection.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.c083 fails because Mara’s genuine, positive relationship with God persists despite her lacking belief that God exists.

objection.text: Elena’s adult son, Tomas, wrongly believes she abandoned him and refuses contact. Elena loves him deeply. She cannot force reconciliation without destroying its voluntary character, so she sends one clear message: she loves him, regrets their separation, and will answer whenever he calls. She keeps the same number, checks for messages, and bears the continuing risk that Tomas will reject her. Her vulnerability consists precisely in remaining genuinely available while leaving his response free. Now imagine a perfectly loving God relating to a resistant person in the same way. The analogy supports P1: perfect love requires an open path to relationship, even though it neither guarantees belief nor compels acceptance. Nothing about this comparison removes love’s exposure to rejection; divine openness is presented as the condition that makes such exposure possible. Thus the analogical route can preserve vulnerable love while supporting P1.
objection.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.c064 fails because a faithful analogy from vulnerable parental love can support P1 without distorting vulnerability into control or guaranteed reciprocation.

objection.text: Consider Mara, a devout but doubting woman who has spent years in a prayerful, trusting relationship with God while never forming the belief that God exists. She attends worship, speaks to God daily, receives what she takes as comfort and direction, and describes the relationship as deeply meaningful. Now suppose the hiddenness argument's conditional premise is granted: if God existed, reasonable nonbelievers in God's existence would be unlikely, so God would have made the relationship available to them. The expectations sub-argument then claims a positively meaningful relationship requires belief that God exists. Mara's case shows that the second premise is false, so the conjunction the missing premise requires is not satisfied. But the missing premise demands that the conditional premise be established and that this second premise be true. Mara's existence refutes the second premise, so the argument fails at the step the missing premise makes necessary, regardless of how the conditional premise fares on either route.
objection.premise_fails_because: The belief requirement fails because a positively meaningful relationship with God can be sustained without belief that God exists, as Mara's case shows.

objection.text: Open theism holds that God's love is genuinely relational: God listens, responds, revises plans in light of creaturely requests, and seeks partners who take part in shaping an open future. Consider Mara, a nurse who is kind, honest and devoted to justice, and who is sincerely convinced there is no God. When her brother falls ill, she does not pray. She asks nothing of God, thanks God for nothing, and never consciously consents to or resists any divine invitation. On the open view, God really would have weighed her petition and could have acted differently because she asked. That opportunity is lost, through no resistance on her part. Her goodness may please God, and God may sustain her. Yet what exists is a one-sided benevolence, not the reciprocal, dialogical partnership open theism places at the heart of divine love. Whatever 'relationship' remains lacks the mutual address and response that make it positively meaningful in the sense at issue. Belief is the minimal condition for being a conversation partner.
objection.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.c083 fails because, on open theism, a positively meaningful relationship with God is reciprocal dialogue in which God responds to creatures' conscious address, and that requires the creature to believe God exists.

objection.text: Skeptical theism denies that we can confidently specify which conditions God requires for a positively meaningful relationship. Imani does not believe God exists; she understands her prayers as private reflection and attributes moral insight solely to human conscience. God silently sustains her and guides her toward generosity, while having reasons beyond her grasp for not making divine reality evident yet. Imani benefits from God’s action, but she neither recognizes nor freely responds to God as a personal other. A relationship requiring mutual personal acknowledgment has not begun, even though grace affects her life. Nothing in our limited grasp of divine purposes licenses the claim that belief is unnecessary for such a relationship.
objection.premise_fails_because: W2072673546.c083 fails because human ignorance of God’s purposes prevents us from asserting that belief is unnecessary for a positively meaningful relationship with God.

turn.speaker: referee
turn.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly supports c064 by arguing that Schellenberg’s analogy distorts Vanstone’s vulnerable conception of divine love. It attacks the claim as stated rather than attributing a different premise or conclusion to the argument.

turn.speaker: referee
turn.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly challenges c041 by defending P1 as an a priori conceptual truth through a purported concept-based judgment, rather than attributing a different premise or conclusion to the argument.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: Your objection is well aimed at the spirit of c064, but it runs together two things. The argument does not say the parental analogy is false of parental love; it says the analogy imports a conception of love (pursuit, control of the beloved's access) that Vanstone's account does not license for God. Your Mara case supports that: her love was self-giving and accepted being unanswered, which is the feature Vanstone stresses. So the analogy's pursuit-based intuition is precisely what needs a warrant when transferred to a vulnerable God. The literature supports the same diagnosis: the hiddenness argument's assumptions about divine love are contestable [W4240083296.a1], and Schellenberg's conception is extrapolated from human love [W2072673546.c030]. Where I must be careful: Mara's case shows that unanswered love can remain vulnerable, but it does not show that a vulnerable God would have no reason to make reciprocation available. The imaging defense suggests a vulnerable God may seek a distinctive relationship while allowing nonresistant nonbelief [W2976724810.a3], and the non-identity reasoning shows divine love can motivate nonbelief without abandoning the beloved [W4415959690.a2]. So the objection shows the analogy is a weak test of Vanstone's view, not that the view forbids pursuit. That is enough to keep c064's conclusion that the analogical route is unsuccessful as a test of the vulnerable conception, though the grounds should be stated as distortion of the test case rather than falsity of parental intuitions.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content:
Your reply concedes the core of my point: once the analogy is said to import pursuit and control, it no longer tests Vanstone's conception but a different one. But you then rest the conclusion on the claim that the pursuit intuition "needs a warrant" when transferred to God. That is a burden-shifting move, and it does not show the analogy distorts Vanstone. Schellenberg can answer that the vulnerable conception still contains a reason to make reciprocation available, which is exactly what the imaging and non-identity references you cite suggest. If so, the analogy is a fair test of a vulnerable God who seeks relationship, and the objection has not been established.

Press the point you left open: Mara's case shows that unanswered love is vulnerable, not that vulnerable love lacks any pursuit-like reason. Your remaining support, that the analogy is "a weak test," is not the same as distortion. To keep c064's conclusion, you need to show that the vulnerable conception rules out the specific reason the analogy invokes, such as an obligation to make the beloved's access to the relationship possible, not merely that it is a different model of love. Until that is shown, I concede the objection does not defeat the analogy, and the grounds for c064 should be restated as a claim about burden of proof rather than misdescription.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that my last reply leaned on a burden-shifting phrase, and I withdraw it. The argument does not say the pursuit intuition needs a warrant merely because it is transferred to God. It says the analogy, as Schellenberg deploys it, builds in a specific structure: the loving agent must make the beloved's access to the relationship available and must not leave the beloved's reciprocation to the beloved's own uptake. Mara's case shows that Vanstone-style love accepts being unanswered and does not treat reciprocation as something the lover is obligated to secure. That is the point of divergence, and it is narrower than 'a different model of love.' The literature supports this only in part. The critique that Schellenberg extrapolates the conception from human love [W2072673546.c030] and that the divine-love assumptions are contestable [W4240083296.a1] shows the analogy needs independent support. But the imaging and non-identity lines [W2976724810.a3; W4415959690.a2] show a vulnerable God can have reasons to permit nonbelief without abandoning the beloved, which blocks the inference from vulnerability to an obligation to pursue. So I concede that the distortion claim does not go through as a strict falsification of the analogy's relevance to Vanstone. What survives is narrower: the analogy's pursuit-to-access premise is not shown to be a faithful part of the vulnerable conception, and Schellenberg has not supplied the warrant. The grounds for c064 should be restated as an unestablished transfer, i.e. a burden-of-proof claim.

Revised premise: Schellenberg's analogical route for P1 is successful only if he independently shows that a vulnerable God is obligated to make the beloved's access to relationship available, rather than merely permitted to do so.
turn.revised_premise: Schellenberg's analogical route for P1 is successful only if he independently shows that a vulnerable God is obligated to make the beloved's access to relationship available, rather than merely permitted to do so.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content: Your Mara case strengthens the point of c064. The defender need not deny that a loving parent may appropriately pursue an estranged adult child, nor deny that such pursuit can make reconciliation available. The narrower claim is that this parental pattern cannot, without further argument, be treated as the criterion for a Vanstone-style divine love. Mara's love for Tom is not deficient merely because it does not manifest as unsolicited pursuit: on the vulnerable model, love can be self-giving precisely by leaving the beloved's freedom—including the freedom not to reciprocate—uncontrolled. Thus, if Schellenberg extrapolates a conception of divine love from a selected pattern of human love [W2072673546.c030], he must show that this pattern captures vulnerability rather than replacing it with a pursuit-based expectation. Your example exposes that missing bridge. This does not establish that divine hiddenness is compatible with every form of perfect love; it establishes that the analogy, by itself, cannot refute the vulnerable conception. That is exactly the limited conclusion of c064 [W2072673546.c064].

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content:
Your reply concedes the central point: the analogy imports a pursuit-based model of love, and c064 only claims that this mismatch blocks the analogy from refuting the vulnerable conception. But the objection was narrower than that, and the reply does not touch the remaining problem. Mara's case shows that the parental pattern is not the only available model of love, yet it does not show that the vulnerable conception is not itself a pursuit-based model in a weaker form. Vanstone's kenotic love still seeks the beloved's good and makes itself available; if availability is part of love, then the analogy's claim that God's silence is evidence against love is not refuted merely by noting that vulnerable love accepts being unanswered.

So I would press the point this way. Your reply needs a principled criterion separating "making reconciliation available" from "pursuit." If the vulnerable conception permits only the first, Schellenberg can ask why God's silence fits that conception rather than merely being tolerated by it. Without that criterion, c064 defeats the analogy only by making it vague, and I would not count it as settled.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You are right that accepting unanswered love does not by itself explain why divine silence counts as making relationship available. The needed distinction is functional, not merely verbal: availability requires that the beloved have an intelligible, non-coercive opportunity to recognize and answer the lover’s self-offer; pursuit adds pressure, repeated intervention, or efforts to overcome refusal. A Vanstone-style love may reject the latter while requiring the former. Mara’s restraint can be vulnerable only if Tom already has a sufficiently available way to receive or decline her love; if he could not even know of her continuing offer, mere non-interference would not establish availability. So c064 correctly identifies that Schellenberg cannot simply extrapolate from a parental pursuit pattern to divine love [W2072673546.c030] and thereby claim to have tested Vanstone’s conception [W2072673546.c064]. But you show that this criticism alone does not establish that hiddenness fits that conception. It blocks the particular analogy; it does not answer Schellenberg’s residual question whether God supplies adequate non-coercive access. The argument’s conclusion that the analogical route is unsuccessful survives only with this more limited reading. If c064 means that vulnerable love can be silent regardless of whether relationship is recognizably available, it does not survive.

Revised premise: Schellenberg’s parental analogy fails to establish P1 unless it shows that perfect vulnerable love requires more than a non-coercive, intelligible opportunity for the beloved to recognize and answer divine self-offer.
turn.revised_premise: Schellenberg’s parental analogy fails to establish P1 unless it shows that perfect vulnerable love requires more than a non-coercive, intelligible opportunity for the beloved to recognize and answer divine self-offer.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: You are right that the verdict about Mara is intuitive and that the concept of perfect love seems to resist needless permanent unknowability. But notice what your case establishes. It shows that a particular conceptual intuition about perfect love is available, not that Schellenberg's specific conditional premise is an a priori necessary truth. Schellenberg needs a claim about the concept of perfect love that is general enough to bind every divine-human relationship, and your Theo case is built to isolate the feature that makes the verdict easy: a beloved who is open, a reachable lover, and a costless reveal. Whether the verdict survives once we ask whether love must seek a conscious reciprocal relationship is the point at issue. The literature offers serious resistance here: perfect love does not require conscious reciprocal relationship on classical accounts [W7168366306.a3], and divine love can be compatible with non-resistant nonbelief because God seeks a distinctive relation of imaging [W2976724810.a3]. Your vignette also presupposes that Mara's refusal is needless, which is exactly what the imaging defense denies in the divine case. So the verdict you reach depends on a premise about needlessness, and that premise is not conceptual in the way Schellenberg requires. I also note that vulnerable love need not require making oneself reachable in every respect, since perfect love is not identical to infinite or constant availability [W4234982327.a2]. I accept that the analogical route is the more fragile one for the author, and the a priori route is where your objection has real force. I do not concede the a priori conditional premise is false, but I concede it is not shown to be a priori by the Theo case.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content:
You say my vignette smuggles in a non-conceptual premise about needlessness. I think it does the reverse: it shows where the conceptual work ends. The a priori claim is conditional: perfect love cannot permit a *needless*, permanent unknowability to an open beloved. Whether God's hiddenness is needless, say because God seeks some distinctive relation of imaging, is a further question about God's reasons. It bears on whether the condition is met, not on whether the conditional is known a priori. So your imaging point moves the dispute to a different premise. It does not show that this one fails.

You also say Theo isolates convenient features. Isolating features is how conceptual testing works. If perfect love really does not require reachability, give me a case that matches Theo's in every relevant respect where the verdict flips. Accounts of love that need no reciprocity must call Mara's love perfect. That is the cost those accounts pay, and you have not yet paid it.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
Your rejoinder is right that needlessness is a question about God's reasons and so bears on whether the condition is met, not on whether the conditional is known a priori. I accept that point and it sharpens my earlier reply. But it cuts against the a priori claim in a way you may not want. If the conditional is a priori only when restricted to needless hiddenness, then the a priori verdict about Mara depends on her refusal being needless, and that is the very thing an imaging theorist disputes [W2976724810.a3]. The Theo verdict is a verdict about a case in which the refusal is stipulated to be needless, so it establishes a restricted conditional, not the unrestricted one Schellenberg's P1 needs to bind every divine-human relationship. On your demand for a matched case: accounts that deny perfect love requires conscious reciprocity do not have to call Mara's love perfect in the sense you intend, because they can locate perfection in the lover's orientation toward the beloved's good [W7168366306.a3] while still rejecting that the refusal is needless. I grant that this is a cost, and that I have not shown the matched case exists. The verdict about Theo is strong and I do not claim it can be dismissed. My position: the a priori route, as stated in c041, is not established by the Theo case, because the case secures only the restricted conditional. Whether the unrestricted conditional is a priori remains open on this evidence.

Revised premise: Schellenberg's conditional premise needs to be restricted to needless divine hiddenness, and the a priori status of that restricted conditional is what the Theo case would have to establish.
turn.revised_premise: Schellenberg's conditional premise needs to be restricted to needless divine hiddenness, and the a priori status of that restricted conditional is what the Theo case would have to establish.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content: Your Mara case is a powerful intuition pump, but it does not by itself yield the modal-conceptual result required. It builds into the description that disclosure is costless, riskless, relationship-promoting, and that delay has no benefit; those are substantive normative and empirical assumptions about what love requires in a particular human caregiving relation. A competent speaker may therefore judge Mara harshly without thereby seeing a contradiction in the very concept of perfect love plus nonbelief. More importantly, Mara is not God: the inference assumes that ideal divine love must seek the same consciously reciprocal relationship that a good human guardian should seek. That assumption is precisely contestable. It is conceivable that one loves another without seeking a personal relationship with them [W2072673546.c039], and classical Christian perfect love need not require conscious reciprocal God-creature relationship [W7168366306.a3]. Nor must a critic first supply God’s reason for hiddenness to challenge the alleged entailment [W2072673546.c009]. Your case may show that the conditional is highly plausible under a human-parental model of love; it does not show that its denial is conceptually impossible across conceptions of divine love. So c041 survives: the a priori route has not established P1, even if the example gives the analogical route renewed argumentative pressure.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content:
You say my stipulations are substantive empirical assumptions about human caregiving. They are not. "Costless, riskless, no benefit from waiting" is simply the case where no good reason for hiding exists. That is exactly the case your side's defenses of hiddenness try to rule out. Stipulating it doesn't smuggle in facts; it isolates the concept.

The revised analogical premise further identifies the relevant remaining burden: Schellenberg must show that perfect vulnerable love obligates God, absent overriding reasons left open in the literature, to keep voluntary relationship genuinely accessible. So your narrowing point improves the presentation: c084 should be read as aggregating independently argued vulnerabilities, not as treating Mara as evidence against both conjuncts. On that reading, the argument survives.

objection.text: Mara, a hospice chaplain, accepts that God exists, committing herself to God's reality and trusting it in practice, but she holds no settled belief on the matter and says so openly. Over years she prays, and in the silence after confession she experiences being answered by a presence that, in her report, acknowledges her by name. Suppose the presence really does respond to her. Then r4 says some person stands in mutual personal acknowledgment with God through accepting rather than believing. The case supports that, since Mara's relationship is explicit and meaningful to her. But r4 needs more: that Mara's acceptance is what secures God's side of the acknowledgment. The case gives no such link. God's acknowledgment could be wholly independent of anything Mara believes or accepts, so the case does not show the second premise false.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise r4 fails because its claim that acceptance supplies mutual acknowledgment is not shown by Mara's case, which establishes only that her relationship is meaningful to her and not that her acceptance, rather than God's own presence, secures the acknowledgment.
